checks.note: Bibliographic details match standard records I know (ARIES TODS 17(1); MVCC TODS 8(4); Codd CACM 13(6); Gupta-Mumick IEEE Data Eng Bull 18(2); Gray-Reuter 1993); checked from memory of standard records, not fetched. The sources support each component (WAL, MVCC, constraints, view maintenance) but none describes this combined design. The mapping is the expert's own composition.

Standard records, from memory. Guarantees (equal leaf depth, half-full non-root nodes, O(log_b N) height) are the textbook B-tree results. The B+ variant (data in leaves) is Comer's survey, not Bayer-McCreight's original, which is a B-tree. The assumptions of independent keys and uniform key size are the expert's gloss, not claims of the papers.

checks.source_as_cited: Bulk loading at a fill factor (practitioner standard; PostgreSQL fillfactor default 90)
checks.note: PostgreSQL btree fillfactor default of 90 matches my knowledge of its docs; not fetched. Sorted bottom-up bulk load is standard. The source honestly names no single paper.

checks.source_as_cited: Yao 1978, On Random 2-3 Trees, Acta Informatica 9
checks.note: Checked via a search record: Acta Inf. 9, 159-170 (1978). The abstract gives storage utilization of about ln 2 (69%) for B-trees of high order. For 2-3 trees themselves the bounds are about 0.70N to 0.79N nodes. So ln 2 holds for high-order B-trees, not for 2-3 trees. The source also assumes random insertion order.
From memory of the standard record. Median split with a separator pushed to the parent is the original algorithm. The 'keys are independent' assumption is the expert's gloss.
From memory: Vol. 3 (1973) section 6.2.4 describes the B*-tree variant of redistribution with 2-to-3 splits and a two-thirds minimum fill. The B*-tree is often credited to Knuth there. Not fetched.
Practitioner standard, honestly labelled. PostgreSQL TOAST stores large values out of line behind a pointer. From memory, not fetched.

From memory of the standard record. B-link trees add right-links and a high key so readers follow the link after a split. Readers take no locks at all in the original algorithm, which is stronger than the claim.

checks.source_as_cited: Lorie 1977, TODS 2(1); Rodeh 2008, ACM Trans. on Storage
checks.note: Rodeh, B-trees, Shadowing, and Clones, ACM TOS 2008, confirmed by a search (a patent citation lists a different venue, but the 2008 ACM copyright notice on the IBM page supports TOS). Lorie 1977 TODS 2(1) from memory. Both describe copy-on-write with old versions kept; Rodeh adds writable clones.

checks.source_as_cited: Mohan et al. 1992, ARIES, ACM TODS 17(1)
checks.note: From memory of the standard record. ARIES is WAL with analysis, redo and undo passes, with fuzzy checkpoints. Durable at commit-record flush is correct. Redo repeats history. The fail-stop assumption is standard.
Standard textbook, from memory (Morgan Kaufmann 1993). Covers atomicity and durability through logging.

From memory. ARIES checkpoints bound restart work, but they are fuzzy: they record the dirty page and transaction tables and are not a complete state snapshot. Redo starts from the minimum recLSN, which can precede the checkpoint record. The claim that a checkpoint is 'complete by construction' is the expert's gloss.

Checked via a search record: CACM 17(9), pp. 530-531, Sept 1974. The result is the square root of twice the checkpoint cost times the mean time to interrupt, which matches the claim. Assumes a fixed checkpoint cost and exponential failures. Daly later refined it.

checks.source_as_cited: Stonebraker 1986, The Case for Shared Nothing, IEEE Database Engineering Bulletin 9(1)
checks.note: Checked via a search record: Database Engineering 9(1), 1986, pp. 4-9. The paper argues shared-nothing is better than shared-memory and shared-disk for scalability. 'Single writer, no locks' is the expert's interpretation. The paper does not prove it, and cross-partition transactions still need coordination.
From memory of the standard record. Read, validation and write phases, with an assumption of low conflict, are what the paper describes. Conflicts are resolved by restarting the transaction.

checks.source_as_cited: Unique key / atomic exclusive create (O_EXCL, Node 'wx')
checks.note: Practitioner standard, from memory. O_CREAT|O_EXCL is atomic on local file systems, and Node's 'wx' flag maps to it. It is not reliable on old NFS. NTFS is fine on a single local volume.

checks.source_as_cited: Codd 1970, CACM 13(6); SQL standard referential actions
checks.note: From memory. Codd 1970 introduces keys and foreign keys. The declared delete actions (restrict, cascade, set null) come from later work and the SQL standard (SQL-92), not from Codd 1970.

checks.source_as_cited: Buneman, Khanna, Tan 2001, Why and Where, ICDT
checks.note: From memory of the standard record (ICDT 2001, LNCS 1973). It defines why- and where-provenance for query results. The assumption that the derivation is a known query matches.

checks.source_as_cited: Gupta & Mumick 1995, IEEE Data Eng. Bull. 18(2)
checks.note: From memory of the standard record. It is a survey of incremental view maintenance and does not say invalidation. The guarantee holds for views with a known defining query.

checks.source_as_cited: Codd 1970; Codd 1972, Further Normalization, in Rustin (ed.), Data Base Systems, Prentice-Hall
checks.note: From memory. Codd 1970 gives first normal form. Codd 1972 (Courant Computer Science Symposia 6) covers 2NF and 3NF. Removing update anomalies is the stated purpose. The assumption that copies are system-produced is the expert's gloss.

checks.source_as_cited: Berenson et al. 1995, A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels, SIGMOD
checks.note: From memory of the standard record. It defines non-repeatable read (P2) and phantom (P3) as phenomena.
From memory. Multiversion concurrency control theory and algorithms, where readers see a consistent version. Snapshot isolation itself is defined by Berenson et al. 1995, not this paper.
Standard textbook, from memory. Defines ACA (avoids cascading aborts) and strict schedules, which guarantee that no reader reads uncommitted data.
From memory. Dirty read (P1/A1) is defined there.

From memory. The paper covers dirty write (P0), dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update (P4), read skew (A5A) and write skew (A5B), plus cursor stability. The completeness-relative-to-catalogue caveat is accurate.
From memory. The book classifies transaction, system and media failures. Torn writes are discussed in its logging and page-integrity material.

From memory of the standard record (System R, SIGMOD 1979). Cost-based access-path selection from stored statistics. The weakness named in the assumptions (statistics that don't match the data) is well known.
From memory. Mid-query re-optimization using statistics collected at checkpoints within the plan, re-planning when estimates are off past a threshold.

Practitioner standard, honestly labelled. OWASP's SQL injection prevention guidance lists parameterised queries as the primary defence. From memory, not fetched. It holds when the interpreter separates code from data, as claimed.

result.overall: All 31 cited sources exist, and no citation had a wrong author, year or venue. I confirmed four by search (Yao 1978, Young 1974, Rodeh 2008, Stonebraker 1986). The rest I judged from standard records and textbook knowledge, with no fetch, so those are weaker evidence. Several claims are stretched. Yao's ln 2 (69%) is for high-order B-trees, not 2-3 trees. ARIES checkpoints are fuzzy, not complete by construction. Codd 1970 gives foreign keys but not the declared delete actions. Stonebraker's paper does not establish "no locks". The D2-whole design is the expert's own composition of components, not a source's result.
